## The founder-emulation items

1. **Who (practitioner `agent`).** YC-C names hotel groups with "call centers and central reservation departments";
   YC-L's video features front-desk staff at a Munich hotel. *My choice:* the reservation agent, central office or
   front desk, who sees the missed-call list. Segment: hotel groups in Germany with a central office or call center.
2. **When (circumstance, occasion, window).** YC-L's "After hours. During peak hours. On holidays." *My choice:* the
   occasion "reservation shift", window the last 7 days (calls come in on every shift; spec 120's "every shift" -> 7
   DAYS), Frequency 5 to 7 days out of 7.
3. **Who pays (decision-maker `director`, Buyer and payer, Purchase friction).** TERMS addresses the hotel group;
   YC-L asks to "book a 10-minute call if you lead a hotel group". *My choice:* the revenue or reservations director
   decides, the hotel's owner has to agree. Purchase friction tests "A data protection review of guest calls" (German
   hotels handle guests' card and personal data on the call); my choice, no source names it.
4. **Mechanism.** YC-C: missed calls forwarded to Codyco, the AI answers, bookings appear in the PMS. Compatibility
   tests call forwarding (the mechanism needs it); Adoption friction tests letting the AI answer in the hotel's voice.
5. **Cost, price, ability.** As in the table. Reading `budget` by the engine (a percent of calls against euros).
6. **Commitment.** TERMS and YC-L: the paid, money-back pilot at one location. The step carries its number ("pay
   €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel"), the gap-8 check.

No first-person account by a German reservation agent or revenue director was found in public (no HN thread; the
site's quotes are curated testimonials). **Every person is the author's invention**, no real person's name is used,
and each is built on the public facts named here.

Revenue directors (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3): Stefanie Wagner (6%), Andreas Keller (4%, below the founder's 5%),
Roberto Bianchi (8%), Ingrid Lindholm (2%, a call center covers after hours), Karim Benali (does not know his rate;
YC-L's "Free AI Strategy Workshop" and SITE's free test number as his ask), Petra Vogel (5%), Hannes Moser (nothing,
would not pay), Joanna Wiśniewska (10% at resort hotels in high season). The value boxes are percents of the calls, in
the founder's unit and period; the price picks are two codes, the pilot's rung and the licence's rung, each placed
against the founder's €3,000 and €1,000.

## Status today

Same idea (SITE, 2026-10-22): "Turn missed hotel calls into paid bookings.", widened to payments, invoices and
handovers; "Running at 15+ hotel groups" (the launch said 7); "€10k+ bookings written directly into the PMS". **No
public price today** (SITE and /faq show none); the €3,000 pilot terms remain the only priced source.

## Open (what could not be sourced, and the workarounds)

- **The licence amount** was never public. €1,000 to €1,500 per hotel a month is the operator's reading of the pilot's
  monthly rate (above). Treat the plan step's reading as a reading of that derivation.
- **Dollars or euros.** YC-L says "$5,000", YC-C "€5,000" for the same hotel; the pilot fee is in euros and the company
  is in Munich, so the entry is in euros. The market is DE, and the golden corpus's rule U (US only) is a note.
- **The "> 8 hotels" / "10 hotels" roll-out threshold** in TERMS and YC-L disagree; the entry does not use it.
- **Job titles.** Neither the agent nor the director is named in public; both are my choices (items 1 and 3).
- **The 5% is the founders' claim** for "the best" offices; no independent figure was sought.
- **UPFRONT_THEN has no "credited" or "money-back" flag**; the fee is a plain up-front amount (header).

insights.line: What would have made a difference?

whys.g1: The two answers say different things (Chiara's real pain is group requests and emails without rates, not phones; Tobias would not hand callers to a machine at all), so leaving each on its own is how a reservation agent would read them and no group exists that either belongs in.

founder.order_why: It runs from where I sell, to the context and window, to the missed-call problem, to how the AI agent fits, beats and starts at a hotel, then to the pilot and who asks, which is how I would explain Codyco to a hotel group.

founder.missing: Nothing asks what it costs or who pays. My 5% missed-call rate, the figure my whole pitch rests on, is not asked as a number either.

screens.why2: My two rows read cleanly after 'Most reservation agents', but Keel's suggestion starts lowercase with 'was allowed', so it does not read whole after that subject and I have to read it twice.

screens.why4: My two rows are distinct and in my words, but the suggested row is clipped and ungrammatical ('was allowed to let'), so one option is odd.
screens.why5: Both of my rows appear exactly as I wrote them, and the extra row is clearly marked as Keel's suggestion, so my meaning is kept.
screens.why7: The picked row on forwarding is treated as an ability (the bar reads 'only sometimes, or no'), but an agent usually cannot set up forwarding on the hotel's phone system, so it should be a permission with 'Only with help or approval'; the card's own example puts this exact condition in the passive with the permission labels, which loses answers like Aylin's old phone system.
screens.instead: Same three rows, with the suggestion fixed to 'Were allowed to let a new tool write bookings into the PMS'; once I pick forwarding, test 'Could unanswered calls have been forwarded to another number?' with the bar 'Holds if no more than 1 in 3 say only with help or approval, or no'.

screens.why1: Right after saying how Codyco fits the desk's day, it is obvious to ask what it does better than today's call-backs and rung-out calls.
screens.why2: Plain to me: one benefit a line, up to four, nine words each, and I wrote my two straight off.
screens.why3: I know exactly what the agents gain over today's way: the calls that rang out become bookings, and callers get answered when the desk is swamped.
screens.why4: The box takes my benefits a line at a time, and 'I'm not sure' is the right way out for a founder who cannot name one.
screens.why5: Nothing is rewritten here; my two benefits stand as I typed them, and the next screen is where I check Keel's version.
screens.why7: It asks for 1 to 4 benefits of up to 9 words each, measured against today's way, with 'I'm not sure' as the founder's escape, which is the card's benefit_list shape.

screens.why1: Right after I typed what Codyco does better, the next step is to check Keel's rows and the belief built from them, and it doesn't repeat anything I already answered.
screens.why2: "Missed calls", "bookings" and "the desk is busy" are everyday words in a German reservations office, and I read it once and understood it.
screens.why3: These are my own benefits, about calls that ring out on a shift, and I know them from the pilot hotels and the missed-call lists.
screens.why4: The two rows overlap, because a caller answered while the desk is busy is just one kind of missed call turned into a booking, and neither row says what beats today's call-back.
screens.why5: The first row is my lead and is kept, but "when the desk is busy" narrows my "after hours, during peak hours, on holidays" to peak alone, and a Sunday-night call that rang out doesn't fit it.
screens.why7: The lead is a row and both rows are in the belief, joined with "and", but the card requires no overlap and these two overlap; a single call that rang out "would have given them missed calls" (plural) also reads oddly, and nothing flags that today's call-back already turns some missed calls into bookings.
screens.instead: Rows: "Missed booking calls turned into bookings" · "Guests answered after hours, at peak and on holidays" · "No call-backs left to chase next morning"; belief: "For most, with it, their last reservation call that rang out unanswered would have given them a booking instead of a lost guest."

screens.why1: Right after what it does better comes what it asks of my agents, which is the natural next question about my solution.
screens.why2: "What will they have to do to start using it" with the hint about setup, extra steps or learning is plain to me, and I answered it straight off in my own words.
screens.why3: I know exactly what my pilot asks of a reservation agent: let the missed calls go to the AI and pick up the calls it hands back to the desk.
screens.why4: It is a free box with the single escape chip *I'm not sure*, which fits a founder who cannot name the effort, and nothing else is offered to go wrong.
screens.why5: My two efforts are kept as I typed them, in *their* voice, and nothing in the frame changes what I meant.
screens.why7: My rows meet the shape (two efforts under 9 words, base-form, *their*), and *Take every call the AI hands to the desk* is a real habit the agent takes on, but the question's "to start using it" and its hint lean towards one-time setup and do not prompt for the new habit of use; and my first row, handing the missed calls over, sits close to the call forwarding Compatibility already tests and to a switch the phone system or IT really makes, which the screen does not steer me away from.
screens.instead: What would your reservation agents themselves have to do, once to set it up or every shift after, to use it? (up to four steps they take themselves, each up to 9 words; not what IT, the director or we set up)

screens.why1: Right after I told Keel what they have to do to start, it shows back the efforts it drafted for me to check, which is where this belongs in the solution step.
screens.why2: 'Missed booking calls', 'the desk' and 'calls the AI hands to the desk' are how my reservation agents and I talk about a shift, so both rows read at once.
screens.why3: Both rows describe what an agent does on their own shift: letting the missed calls go to the AI and picking up the calls it passes back.
screens.why4: Two distinct efforts, in my words, in the 'their' voice, each under 9 words, with nothing nonsensical and nothing missing that I would need.
screens.why5: It still says what I typed: my agents let missed calls go to the AI and take the handovers back at the desk.
screens.why7: The second row is a clean new habit of use the agent takes themselves, but 'Hand their missed booking calls to the AI' leans on the call forwarding Compatibility already tests and on a switch the director or IT sets up, so one rule is bent.
screens.instead: Keep 'Take every call the AI hands to the desk' and replace the first row with an effort only the agent takes, e.g. 'Check the AI's new bookings in the PMS each shift'.

screens.why1: Right after I checked the adoption steps, it makes sense to ask which one is most likely to stop my reservation agents, and that one gets tested.
screens.why2: Both rows are in our words on the desk (missed booking calls, the AI handing a call to the desk); only the intro's 'nothing is reworded here' reads as Keel talking about itself.
screens.why3: An agent knows from their own shifts whether they would let missed calls go to an AI and whether they would take its handovers.
screens.why4: The two rows are separate efforts, one letting go of the missed calls and the other a new habit of taking handovers, and the escape is mine to use, so nothing is missing or doubled.
screens.why5: Both rows are the revision-25 wording I accepted, and my pick, handing the missed calls to the AI, is exactly what I believe will stop them.
screens.why7: Both rows are base-form, one voice, the agent's own and on the one measure, and the belief can go either way; but 'hand their missed booking calls to the AI' leans on a forwarding setup and a go-ahead that in a hotel group the director or IT controls, so it bends the 'a step they take themselves' rule and brushes Compatibility's forwarding row.
screens.instead: Which one is most likely to stop them? -- Let the AI answer guests in our hotel's name when the desk can't pick up · Take every call the AI hands to the desk, mid-shift

screens.why1: Just before the study goes out is the obvious place to decide whether respondents get an ask at the end, and nothing earlier asked it.
screens.why2: "Offer a pilot?" with Yes or No is plain to me; pilot is my own word for the first step with a hotel group, and the hint shows the exact line people will see.
screens.why3: Whether I want leads from this study is my own call, and I can answer it at once.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover the choice, they are distinct and in plain words, and a binary setting needs no escape chip.
screens.why5: My pilot is a paid, money-back €3,000 trial at one hotel that the revenue director signs, but the line shown is a free email sign-up put to reservation agents who cannot commit a hotel, so the word pilot drifts from what I typed.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? People who say yes get a line at the end: "Would your hotel try this on its missed booking calls at one location? Leave your email and we'll reach whoever decides."

screens.why1: Choosing who asks the questions belongs right before launch, once the study is written and the pilot offer set.
screens.why2: Two named voices with a 5-second sample, a flat 400-credit cost and an SMS link are clear on first read.
screens.why3: As the founder I can judge which voice my reservation agents would talk to, after hearing each for five seconds.
screens.why4: Two voices is a fair choice, but nothing says whether Daphne or Saskia speaks German, which matters most for agents at German hotel groups; the hint also calls it a voice while my recorded pick says face.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product, my numbers or the agent and director roles changes or leaks on this screen.
screens.instead: Who should ask reservation agents your questions, in German? Daphne (DE) ▶ Hear · 5 s / Saskia (DE) ▶ Hear · 5 s, with the face and voice recorded once for 400 credits.

screens.why1: Right after choosing who asks the agents, choosing how they answer is the natural last step before sending, and it matters for agents who read the link between calls on a busy shift.
screens.why2: Video, typing and tapping are plain to me, and an AI that talks to people is exactly my own business, so 'AI interviewer · Daphne' needs no second read.
screens.why3: I know my agents sit at a desk or in a central office with a headset on and a phone that keeps ringing, so I can judge that read-and-tap suits them better than talking to a video.
screens.why4: The three options cover voice, text and letting each agent decide, they do not overlap, and the descriptions say what each one means for the person answering.
screens.why5: My pick 'Read and tap' is shown as typed, and nothing of Codyco, the AI receptionist or the director's role leaks into how the agents are asked.

screens.why1: After choosing how agents answer, deciding who gets the link is the obvious last step before sending.
screens.why2: Plain founder words; 'Contacts page' is Keel's own page I would just have seen in the app.
screens.why3: I know whether I am sending to reservation agents I know at our 7 hotel groups or posting in a hoteliers' group.
screens.why4: Three distinct ways to reach people, covering named contacts, a Keel list and an open group link, with nothing missing for my case.
screens.why5: Nothing of my idea is changed or leaked here; it is a delivery choice and my pick 'people I know by name' sits as the first option.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits under the title with the tally '3 beliefs: 3 holding', and each card shows its own count against the bar of 5 of 7, so I can see the weakest card, Relative advantage at exactly 5 of 7, is what decides it.
screens.why_b2: Each card says plainly what was counted ('said yes, easily or most of the time', 'would do it'), over 7 people, and where the bar sits (5 of 7), and 'at the bar' flags the one that only just made it.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility and Adoption friction are my beliefs as I checked them, but the statement under the title is garbled ('the hotel's reservation agents the hotel forwards the call... and gets back') and the Relative advantage line ('would have given them missed calls turned into bookings') is clumsy, though I still recognise them.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the page says what holding means for Codyco or what to do next, such as moving to the pilot, or that Relative advantage only just cleared the bar and needs another look; 'What it measures' explains the method, not the next step.
screens.why_b5: The n of 7 stays visible and 'at the bar' and '3 on a condition' are disclosed, but calling all three 'Holding up' without saying that 7 people is a small sample and that half the adopters had conditions reads a bit stronger than the data carries.
screens.instead: Holding up with 7 agents, just: the advantage cleared the bar with nothing to spare (5 of 7) and 3 of the 6 who'd hand over calls want conditions, so ask those conditions in the €3,000 pilot pitch before calling it settled.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "6 of 7 said yes, easily or most of the time · bar 5 of 7", so I see both the verdict and the number that decides it at once.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the four answers over 7 people, and the strip shows 6 for, 1 against and the marker at 5 with the 1-in-3 rule, so all three are plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility and "could forward unanswered calls to another number" are my row, though the bar line "You said could forward..." is missing its subject and the belief drops "at hotel groups".
screens.why_b4: It tells me concretely that forwarding is not the blocker and sends me to Adoption friction, the card I should open next.
screens.why_b5: It does say a small group is a lean, not a call, but the So line then states flatly that forwarding "is not what will stop them"; Aylin's quote (IT has to change it, the owner won't pay) is a needs-approval case, yet it is filed under an ability label, "Only sometimes", which softens the one real compatibility risk among only 7 people.
screens.instead: Holding up, a lean from 7: 6 of 7 could forward their missed calls; the one who couldn't has an old phone system that needs IT and the owner's money, so ask about the phone system on the first call with every group. Adoption friction, below, looks like the bigger risk.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 5 of 7 for against a bar of 5 of 7, marked at the bar, so I know it held and by exactly what margin.
screens.why_b2: Count, n and bar are all there, but 'Better · 5 5 a lot' runs together and the chart's 'Same' isn't the 'No difference' my respondents picked, so I read it twice.
screens.why_b3: It's my dimension and my two benefits on the last reservation call that rang out unanswered, though the bar line quotes only the first benefit.
screens.why_b4: Pointing me to Adoption friction is useful, but it doesn't say that one more no-difference flips this, or that a group whose call center already covers after hours is where my pitch is weakest.
screens.why_b5: It calls 7 people a lean, not a call, and says at the bar rather than strong, though the count line's 'their last booking call' is looser than the question actually asked.
screens.instead: Holding up, just: 5 of 7 said a lot better, but one more no-difference would sink it; the no-difference came from a group whose call center already takes after-hours calls, so lead with groups that have no night cover.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "6 of 7 would do it · bar 5 of 7 · 3 on a condition", so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the four answers over 7 people, and the strip shows 6 for, 1 against, with the marker at 5. The bar is restated as "no more than 1 in 3 say probably not or no", which still squares with 5 of 7 at a glance.
screens.why_b3: Adoption friction and "Most would hand their missed booking calls to the AI" are the row I checked. Only the bar line's "You said hand their..." reads clumsily.
screens.why_b4: The So line just splits 3 as is and 3 on a condition, then points below to a list that repeats the same condition. It never says what that means for me, such as proving in the pilot that bookings land correctly in the PMS.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible, the small group is called "a lean, not a call", and the 3 conditional yeses are kept apart from the plain yeses rather than folded into a strong hold.
screens.instead: Holding up, but only 3 of 7 would hand the calls over as is; 3 more need to trust the bookings come out right, so make booking accuracy in the PMS the thing the pilot proves.

screens.why_b1: Each box states its verdict ('Compatibility held, 6 of 7', 'Relative advantage held, 5 of 7') with the deciding count and the bar right beside the status word.
screens.why_b3: The Compatibility belief is my row as I checked it, but the Relative advantage belief is a stitched sentence ('their last reservation call that rang out unanswered would have given them missed calls turned into bookings...') that I recognise but would never say.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the screen says what to do: no line about phone systems that can't forward, or about groups whose call center already covers the evenings.
screens.why_b5: The n of 7 stays visible and 'at the bar' is honest, but the heading calls Aylin 'the 1 who said no' when her pick was 'Only sometimes', and nothing says that 7 people is a small read or that one more 'no' would sink Relative advantage.
screens.why_b6: The quotes give me what I didn't type: an old phone system blocked by IT and an owner who won't pay, guests who want a person who knows the house, and a group whose call center covers after six while the real pain is group emails with no rates.
screens.instead: Relative advantage held right at the bar, 5 of 7, so one more no would have broken it; the two against already cover after-hours or won't hand guests to a machine, so pitch groups without evening cover, and for old phone systems offer the forwarding setup yourself.

screens.why1: As the first screen it obviously checks that I'm the right person, an agent in a hotel group's central reservations, before asking anything about my calls.
screens.why2: Central reservations office and call center are the words we use for where I sit in Munich, so I'd answer at once.
screens.why3: It asks where I work, which I know without thinking.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it cleanly for a gate, and no escape fits since a gate has none.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's segment of German hotel groups' central reservations offices or call centers, and nothing of the product leaks.
screens.why6: It is short, one question, and easy to answer on one hearing, though the screener's own spoken close is just 'Yes or no.' rather than 'I'll read 2 options.'

screens.why1: Right after confirming I work in a central reservations office, asking whether a call went unanswered this week is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: I understand it, but in our office we talk about 'lost' or 'abandoned' calls in the queue, not a call 'ringing out', so I need a second to map it to what I see on the wallboard.
screens.why3: Calls come to me through the queue, not to my own phone, so I would answer from the wallboard's abandoned count and partly guess whether that counts as 'my' call ringing out.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it cleanly, and the chips belong to the story box after a Yes, not to this gate.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's 'not every call gets answered' as one act, and nothing about a product or their terms reaches me.
screens.why6: It is one short sentence followed by 'Yes or no.', which is easy to hear once and answer.
screens.why7: Two fixed answers with no escape, the window is named, and it asks about the event, not the routine: a colleague on a quiet, well-staffed week with no abandoned calls can truly say No, while one on a trade-fair Saturday says Yes.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did a reservation call you could have taken hang up in the queue before anyone answered? Yes · No

screens.why1: Right after asking whether a call rang out unanswered, showing me the idea for those missed calls is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: PMS, OPERA Cloud, Sihot and Apaleo are the systems I work in every day, so it reads plainly to me; only 'in the hotel's voice' is a bit vague.
screens.why3: I sit in the group's central office taking calls for many hotels, so 'your hotel forwards calls' and 'calls nobody at the hotel picks up' are framed from a single property's desk rather than from my office, and I'd have to translate it to my situation.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: It says plainly what the product does and what the builders believe, with no internal labels for people leaking through.
screens.why6: Heard once, 'calls nobody picks up' comes three times, and the fragment 'That is OPERA Cloud, Sihot or Apaleo' sounds clipped and suggests those are the only systems.
screens.instead: Imagine Codyco, an AI reservation agent for the calls your office doesn't get to. Calls that ring out go to it; it answers the guest in your hotel's voice, takes payment and books straight into your PMS, such as OPERA Cloud, Sihot or Apaleo, and passes a call to your desk by rules you set. The people building it believe it would take the calls nobody picks up.

screens.why1: Right after the Codyco card, asking whether our missed calls could go somewhere else is the obvious next question, because that is how such an agent would get them.
screens.why2: The words are plain to me, but 'think of your last booking call' points me at a call I answered, and then it asks about my unanswered calls, so I have to read it twice to know which moment it means.
screens.why3: In our central office the overflow routing in the phone system is set by the team lead or IT, not by me at my headset, so I would be half guessing about what could have been done.
screens.why4: 'Yes, most of the time' and 'Only sometimes' don't fit a phone setting that is either switched on or not, and my true answer is missing: only if the team lead or IT sets it up.
screens.why5: Nothing leaks beyond the idea card shown on purpose, and the condition reads as forwarding missed calls to another number, which is what the idea needs.
screens.why6: It is short, one question, and four short options plus 'you can't tell' are easy to hold when heard once.
screens.why7: Forwarding is an act someone else sets up for the agent, so it is a permission, but it is served on the ability scale in the active voice. That drops 'Only with help or approval' and the passive stem the card prescribes, though the condition itself still splits people for and against.
screens.instead: Think of your last booking call. Could unanswered calls have been forwarded to another number? Yes, easily · Yes, with some steps · Only with help or approval · No · I can't tell

screens.why1: Right after the idea card it makes sense to ask whether this thing would have helped with the call that rang out, which is exactly what I said happened this week.
screens.why2: The words are mine, but 'done that better' has me pausing: done what better, the call nobody picked up? I'd read it as 'would it have handled that call better', but only on a second read.
screens.why3: I know that call: on a fair Saturday the queue backs up and a guest who rang out is a booking we probably lost to the hotel down the road, so I can judge whether something answering it would have helped.
screens.why4: A lot better, a little better, no difference or worse covers it, with nothing overlapping, and 'I can't tell' fits because I don't know how well a machine would really handle a booking call.
screens.why5: It names Codyco as shown on the idea card and adds nothing more about the product. 'AI reservation agent' is a bit close to my own job title, but it's their own label, given openly.
screens.why6: Heard once, it's one question with four short options I can hold and the escape said last.
screens.why7: Code's four fixed answers are in order, two for and two against, so the belief can be supported or refuted. 'I can't tell' is the one escape, apart, and the hard case is the call that rang out, not just any call.
screens.instead: Think of the last reservation call that rang out unanswered at your office. Would Codyco, an AI reservation agent, have handled that call better for you, or not? A lot better · A little better · No difference · Worse · I can't tell

screens.why1: After the idea and whether it would do better, asking whether I'd actually take it on is the natural last question.
screens.why2: Missed booking calls and handing them over are words we use on the floor, so I understand it on first hearing.
screens.why3: Where unanswered calls get routed is set in the phone system by our team lead or IT, not by me, so my yes or no is partly a guess about something I don't control.
screens.why4: Yes, a real condition about guests' bookings being correct, probably not and no are distinct and cover what I'd say, and I can't tell fits.
screens.why5: Only the idea card's own words reach me; nothing of the founder's plan or terms leaks.
screens.why6: Short, one question, four short options spoken as a list and one escape, easy to hold.
screens.why7: The options and escape have the right shape, but the effort is half another role's setup (call routing) and nearly repeats screen 4's forwarding question, which is Compatibility's ground, rather than a step or habit I take myself.
screens.instead: To use Codyco, you'd check the bookings it took while you were busy, at the start of each shift. Would you do that, or not? Yes · Only if it flags the ones it wasn't sure of · Probably not · No · I can't tell
